title: Restraint of speech (ch. 6)
hook: silence is valued even in good talk

segments.voice: Yesterday, obedience: a ready yes, without the speech running underneath. Your line was no murmuring. Did you catch the speech before it started? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-three.

A meeting, a dinner table, a group chat. Someone says something, and there's a good reply ready on your tongue. Not a cruel one. A true one, even a kind one. Then a beat passes, and the moment moves on, and the reply never gets said. Was something lost? A rule for monks would be expected to warn about bad words: gossip, lies, cutting remarks. Saint Benedict's Rule does. But chapter six goes somewhere stranger. It says that sometimes even good words are better left unsaid, for the sake of silence. Today: restraint of speech.
screen: `A GOOD REPLY, READY TO GO.` → `THE MOMENT PASSES.` → `EVEN GOOD WORDS CAN WAIT.`

segments.voice: Benedict opens the chapter with a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "I said: I will take heed to my ways: that I sin not with my tongue." The psalm goes on to say the speaker held his peace, even from good things. Benedict takes that seriously. If the psalmist kept back even good words for the sake of silence, he reasons, how much more should we keep back the harmful ones. So silence here isn't only a fence against sin. It's valued for itself. Then he leans on Proverbs. Talk a great deal, Proverbs warns, and you won't escape sin. And a sharper line: "Death and life are in the power of the tongue." Words aren't weightless. They build people and they break them. Next comes a line about roles. In the monastery, Benedict says, speaking and teaching belong to the teacher; being quiet and listening belong to the disciple. So when a monk needs something from his superior, he asks humbly, with respect. And one kind of talk he shuts out everywhere: coarse jokes and idle chatter meant only to get a laugh. Here's what's easy to miss. Benedict doesn't ban speaking. Monks talk, ask, teach, sing the psalms aloud. The chapter is about restraint, not total silence. It's a rationing of words, so the ones that do get said can carry weight. And a person who speaks less has more room to listen, to others and, Benedict would add, to God.
screen: `TAKE HEED, THAT I SIN NOT WITH MY TONGUE.` · `EVEN GOOD WORDS, FOR SILENCE'S SAKE.` · `THE TEACHER SPEAKS. THE DISCIPLE LISTENS.` · `NOT A BAN. A RATIONING.` · then, large: `DEATH AND LIFE ARE IN THE POWER OF THE TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak less today, starting by practicing it now. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one conversation coming up today. A call, a meeting, supper. Run it in your mind, and notice where you'd usually add more: the extra explanation, the joke to fill a pause, the point already made once. Pick one of those and, in your mind, leave it out. Let the pause stay a pause. Then just sit in the quiet you have right now, with nothing to say to anyone. If you pray, you can let the silence itself be the prayer. The bell holds the time.
Restraint of speech. Not a vow of silence, but a habit of holding back, so that the words that remain carry weight. Today's word.
Your line: fewer words. Today, in one conversation, say what's needed and stop. Let one good sentence go unsaid, and see what fills the space. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Benedictine communities keep times and places of quiet, and Catholic retreat houses often ask guests to keep silence for part or all of a retreat.

pairs: in the power of the tongue

myth: chapter six bans monks from speaking at all
monks talk, ask, teach and sing. the chapter rations words; it doesn't forbid them.
Benedict says even good words are sometimes better left unsaid
following the psalm, he values silence even over good talk.
in the Rule, a monk with a question shouldn't ask it
he asks humbly and with respect; listening is the disciple's part.

fork.setup: you're a monk with a true, kind thing to say, but the room has fallen quiet. what does chapter six lean toward?
options: say it: good words should always be spoken.
sometimes let even a good word go, for the sake of silence.
say it, and add a joke to lighten the quiet.
fork.reveal: Benedict reads the psalm this way: even good words are sometimes held back for silence's sake, and jokes meant only for laughs are shut out.

original.note: Latin, the word in the chapter's title: holding back from speech.

trapdoor: what you thought: monks take a vow of silence.
what it means: chapter six rations speech, holding back even good words at times, so the words that remain carry weight.
what a scholar hears: the chapter's title word is taciturnitas, restraint in speaking, and it builds on Psalm 38 and Proverbs.
